title: Organic vs Conventional Meat and Milk
summary: Skeptic blog post arguing the higher omega-3 found in organic meat and milk comes from grass feeding, is too small in absolute terms to matter, and rests on weak meta-analyses.

assertions.quote: levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) and omega-3 fatty acids are higher in the organic versions of both.
Grass fed conventional meat and milk has the same profile as grass-fed organic.
even a 50% relative increase in this small amount likely has few health implications.

verdicts.note: Milk and red meat supply little omega-3, so even a large relative increase adds a small share of recommended intake.

Half a litre of full-fat milk supplies an estimated 39 mg (organic) vs 25 mg (conventional) of very long-chain n-3, 16% vs 11% of the recommended intake: a small absolute gain, though the authors frame it as a useful complementary source and no outcome data exist.
Switching to organic dairy and meat would raise dietary omega-3 by an estimated 2.5-8% and 2.5-4%; the review calls the effect minor with no specific health benefits derivable.

assertions.quote: The net effect of eating grass-fed beef on your fatty acid profile is going to be negative.
Organic techniques are based on the appeal to nature, not an evidence-based approach to best practices.

verdicts.note: This is a framing judgment about the philosophy behind organic standards.

assertions.quote: Organic is still not any better
